**Sentence 1: Row space and nullspace**

The row space of a matrix A is the set of all linear combinations of the rows of A. The nullspace of A is the set of all vectors x such that Ax = 0.

To see why this is true, consider the equation Ax = 0. This equation says that the linear combination of the rows of A, with coefficients from x, equals the zero vector. Since the rows of A are linearly independent (by definition of a matrix), the only way for this equation to hold is if all the coefficients are 0. This means that x is orthogonal to each row of A.

Now, the second part of the sentence claims that the product of x with any combination of rows of A must be 0. This is true because if x is orthogonal to each row of A, then the dot product of x with any linear combination of rows of A will also be 0. This is because the dot product is linear in the second argument (the rows of A), so if x is orthogonal to each row, the result will be 0.

**Sentence 2: Column space and left nullspace**

The column space of a matrix A is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of A. The left nullspace of A is the set of all vectors x such that xA = 0.

The statement claims that the column space of A is orthogonal to the left nullspace of A. This means that if you take any vector x in the left nullspace and project it onto any column of A, the result will be the zero vector. In other words, the dot product of x with each column of A is 0.

The statement claims that the row space of AT is perpendicular to the nullspace of AT.
